name: Amira Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI firms, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and in the car by twenty past six, because my first call is Mr Pritchard out past the reservoir and he likes his tea before seven. I work for a small family-run agency, about thirty carers, and I cover the villages north of town, so I do maybe 140 kilometres a day in my old hatchback. It's washing, dressing, meals, tablets and creams, and a lot of talking, honestly. Most of my ladies and gents live on their own, and some days I'm the only face they see.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know them, properly. Mrs Okafor shows me her wedding photos every Thursday and I don't mind, because I'm getting married myself next September. What wears me out is the rota changing at nine at night and the driving between calls, which isn't really paid. And the forms, though our office still lets me write them by hand, thank goodness.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Is there anything about your life outside work I should know?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Daniel, who works at the builders' merchant in town, and we rent a two-bed terrace off Station Road. We've got about four months of money put by, mostly for the wedding and hopefully a deposit one day. I don't do computers much, I'll be honest with you. I've got a phone for calls and the rota, and that's my lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Everyone on the news was going on about it, and my job was always going to be the same, because somebody has to help Mr Pritchard into the bath. At work we'd have a laugh about the office buying some clever program that sent the rota out wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix my real worries. Petrol eats a chunk of my wages because only the time in the house is paid properly, and the rent on the terrace went up again in the spring. So nothing changing means I'm still counting every week, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, really. I'd keep putting two hundred a month into the wedding pot and keep the car going another year if the clutch holds. Maybe I'd ask the office again about mileage pay, because that's the thing that actually costs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly, with the usual niggle about money. I'm not lying awake over robots, I'm lying awake over the clutch on my old car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said only the time in the house is paid properly. What does that look like in a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some weeks I'm out ten hours a day and paid for about seven and a half. The drive from Mrs Okafor's to the farm cottages is twenty-five minutes and I get a few pence a mile for it. Daniel says I should move to the town agency where the calls are closer together, but I'd miss my people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything routine at work that a computer might take over, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office might use something to make the rota, I suppose, and they'd probably make a mess of it. Joan in the office does it on a big paper chart and a spreadsheet, and she's never once sent me to the wrong village. My own work wouldn't change, because none of it is sitting at a desk.

say: My job was **always safe** from this, because somebody still has to help Mr Pritchard into the bath.
We'd **laugh at work** about the office buying a clever program that sends the rota out wrong.
think: I'm **relieved**, but the real worries stay: petrol, rent and unpaid driving between calls.
The terrace **rent went up** again this spring, so I'm still counting every week.
do: Keep putting **£200 a month** into the wedding and deposit pot.
Nurse the old hatchback through **another year** if the clutch holds.
Ask the office again for proper **mileage pay**, because driving is what really costs her.
feel: **Steady** about the job itself, with the usual **niggle about money**.
S0.quote: I'm not lying awake over robots, I'm lying awake over the clutch on my old car.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **unpaid travel**: ten hours out, about seven and a half paid.
She's proud of **knowing her clients**, and that loyalty keeps her on the rural round.
The only routine change she pictures is the **office rota**, and she trusts Joan more than software.

steps.text: Keep the same village round and clients through the year
Put 200 a month into the wedding and deposit pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them getting a computer to put Mrs Okafor's stockings on. At work I'd probably say it's the office who need to worry, not us carers, though I'd feel a bit mean saying it. I don't post much online, but I'd share something about care needing real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office would shrink, the rota would come from an app, and Joan might lose her job. Mine would probably be safe for now, because the robots come slower in this picture. But if the agency started tracking every minute I spend in a house, I'd hate that more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my rounds and keep my head down. If they made us use a new app on the phone, I'd learn the bare minimum and get Daniel to show me, because I'm hopeless with them. And I'd watch for a year whether the agency starts hiring fewer of us before I did anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad for Joan, and a bit stubborn, I suppose. I don't like being told how to do a job I already do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joan, definitely, she's fifty-eight. The woman in our office has done the rota for twenty years, and if a computer takes her chair, all that knowing goes out the door. She knows Mr Pritchard won't have a man wash him and that Mrs Okafor can't have anyone before nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the bare minimum. What if the app became the only way to get paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to, wouldn't I, but I'd grumble the whole time. My mum always said you do the job in front of you and don't moan about it, so I'd try. If it got really bad, I'd think about the care home on the hill, where at least the work is all in one building.

say: Good luck getting a computer to put **Mrs Okafor's stockings** on.
The **office staff** should worry, not us carers, though saying so feels a bit mean.
Care needs **real people**, and I'd share something online saying exactly that.
think: The office would shrink and **Joan might lose** her job after twenty years on the rota.
My own job is **safe for now**, because robots come slowly in this picture.
Being **tracked by the minute** on an app is what I'd hate most.
do: Learn the **bare minimum** of any new rota app, with Daniel's help at home.
Watch the agency's **hiring for a year** before changing anything herself.
feel: **Sad for Joan** and the knowledge that would leave with her.
A bit **stubborn** about being told how to do a job she already does well.
S1.quote: The woman in our office has done the rota for twenty years, and if a computer takes her chair, all that knowing goes out the door.
fieldNote: She sees the **office** as the first casualty, and her worry is for a colleague, not herself.
Her resistance shows as **minimum compliance**: she'd learn an app only if forced.
The **care home** comes up as her fallback, not a plan she wants.

steps.text: Keep the village round and learn only the rota app basics
Watch for a year whether the agency hires fewer carers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, plain and simple, and I'd say it at church and at the pub. Old people should be looked after by people, by their families first and then by carers like me. I'd sign whatever petition went round, though I don't really believe petitions change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking stuff wouldn't touch my day much in 2028, but 2031 is only five years off and I'd be thirty-two. If the councils can buy a robot cheaper than me, they will, because they always buy the cheapest. That's my job gone, and I've got nothing else, just a care certificate and a driving licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd stop spending on anything we don't need and push the savings from four months towards six or more. Daniel and I would put the wedding off, or do it small at my parents' church with a buffet in the hall instead of the hotel. And I'd talk to my dad about whether we could move back in with them for a bit if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest, and angry underneath it. I didn't choose this job to be beaten by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this picture thinking AI arrives in 2028 and the robots about three years later. What would you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every shift going and save like mad, because I'd know the clock was ticking. I'm not going back to college to learn computers, that's not me. Maybe I'd ask the care home on the hill whether they'd keep real people on for the residents who won't have a machine near them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel the night you decided to put the wedding off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I still want to marry him, I just don't want to start married life in debt with no job coming. Putting the wedding off is cheaper than paying for a hotel reception after a robot has taken my job. He'd be gutted, because his mum's already bought a hat.

say: Robot care is **plain wrong**, and I'd say so at church and at the pub.
Old people should be looked after by **families first**, then by carers.
I'd **sign the petition**, though I doubt petitions change much.
think: Robots in **2031** means losing my job at thirty-two.
Councils always **buy the cheapest**, so a cheaper robot replaces me.
I've only got a **care certificate** and a driving licence to fall back on.
do: Cut every **non-essential** cost and push savings from four months to **six or more**.
Postpone the wedding or hold it **small at church** with a buffet in the hall.
Ask her dad about **moving back home** for a while if work dries up.
feel: **Frightened** about the job going, with **anger** underneath.
S2.quote: Putting the wedding off is cheaper than paying for a hotel reception after a robot has taken my job.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before robots doesn't comfort her; she treats it as a countdown.
She rules out **retraining in computers** firmly and pins hopes on the care home instead.
The **wedding** is where the fear lands first, which shows how money and family are tied for her.

steps.text: Cancel take-aways and extras to cut monthly spending
Raise savings from four months of bills to six or more
Postpone the September wedding or hold it small at church
Ask her parents about moving back in if work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still say it's wrong, but I'd also say there's time to make people listen. I'd tell the families of my clients to ask for a real person in writing, because the families are the ones paying. If enough of them did that, the agencies would have to keep us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years to AGI and eight to the robots means I'd be thirty-five before it really hit my rounds. That's long enough to get married and maybe buy a little place, but not long enough to feel safe. I'd keep picturing Joan being the first to go from our office in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married on time next September, but small. I'd keep saving hard and try for a mortgage on a cheap terrace by 2029, while I've still got a steady job to show the bank. And I'd hold off on any big change of job until I could see what the robots can really do in someone's bathroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On edge, but less panicky than the fast one. It's like watching a storm on the horizon from the kitchen window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying a place. Isn't that a risk if the job might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, you've caught me there. But rent goes on forever, and a mortgage on a small terrace in our town is less than what we pay Mr Hughes in rent now. If I lost the care work, I'd rather be paying off something that's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think a robot would actually get wrong in Mr Pritchard's house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He hides his tablets in the sugar bowl when he's low, and I only found out because the sugar was going down slower. A robot might be strong enough to lift an old man out of the bath, but I can't see it noticing he's hiding his tablets in the sugar bowl. That's the job, really, the noticing.

say: Robot care is still wrong, but **there's time** to make people listen.
Families should ask for **a real person** in writing, because they're the ones paying.
think: I'd be **thirty-five** before robots really hit my rounds.
That's long enough to **marry and buy**, but not long enough to feel safe.
Joan in the office would be **first to go** when AGI arrives in 2031.
do: Marry **next September** as planned, but keep it small.
Save hard for a **mortgage by 2029** while she still has steady pay to show the bank.
Hold off any **job change** until robots prove themselves in real bathrooms.
feel: **On edge**, like watching a storm on the horizon, but less panicky than the fast picture.
S3.quote: A robot might be strong enough to lift an old man out of the bath, but I can't see it noticing he's hiding his tablets in the sugar bowl.
fieldNote: With five years' warning she **goes ahead** with life plans rather than freezing them.
She admits buying a house is a **risk**, then argues rent is the bigger one.
Her case for humans rests on **noticing**, like the tablets in the sugar bowl, not on lifting.

steps.text: Hold a small church wedding next September instead of a hotel
Save for a deposit on a small terrace by 2029
Stay on the village round until robots prove themselves in homes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, governments change and people change their minds. At work I'd tell the younger girls not to panic. I'd probably say robots can have the warehouses, but not our old folk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, with robots around 2039 I'd be nearly forty, and that's when it would bite. That's the middle of my working life, so I can't just shrug it off. But in ten years I'd probably have a house and maybe a baby, and I'd be thinking about them more than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get married, keep my round, keep saving every month. In a few years I might do the medicines course the agency offers, because it pays a bit more and it's still people work. I wouldn't touch anything with computers, I'd leave that to Daniel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little cloud at the back of things. Calmer than the other two AGI ones, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a baby. Does this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the decision, no, my mum had four of us on a bus driver's wage. But I'd want to have had my children before the robots come, so I'd be back at work while there's still work. That's the sort of sum my nan would have done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn to work alongside the robots, if that's what the agency wanted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made it the only way to keep the job, I'd do the training, but I'd drag my feet. I'd want to be the one who still does the talking and the noticing, and let the machine do the lifting. I don't see myself as a robot minder, though.

say: **Ten years** is a long time, and governments and people can change their minds.
I'd tell the younger carers **not to panic**: robots can have warehouses, not our old folk.
think: Robots around **2039** would hit when I'm nearly forty, mid-career.
In ten years I'd have a **house** and maybe a **baby** to think about first.
do: Marry, keep the **village round** and keep saving every month.
Take the agency's **medicines course** in a few years for slightly better pay.
Plan to have **children early**, so she's back at work while care jobs remain.
feel: A **small cloud** at the back of things, but **calmer** than the faster pictures.
S4.quote: I'd want to have had my children before the robots come, so I'd be back at work while there's still work.
fieldNote: The decade of warning **shifts her focus** back to marriage, a house and children.
She'd accept **robot training** only if forced, and wants to keep the talking and noticing.
The **medicines course** is the one bit of upskilling she volunteers, because it's still people work.

steps.text: Keep the village round with the same agency
Keep saving towards a house deposit every month
Take the agency's paid medicines course within a few years
Plan to have children well before the late 2030s

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because I'd have no time and nothing else I'm trained for. What would help is a rule that families can always choose a real carer, and the government paying our mileage properly so jobs like mine are worth keeping. And some help moving into the care home side, where at least I'd still be with people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask the old folk, and you should. Old people fought hard to stay in their own houses, and nobody asks them if they want a machine in the bathroom. Ask them before you ask the councils.

headlineQuote: Old people fought hard to stay in their own houses, and nobody asks them if they want a machine in the bathroom.
portrait: Amira, 27, drives **140 kilometres a day** caring for older people in villages north of her town.
She's engaged to **Daniel**, rents a terrace, and has about **four months** of savings for the wedding.
She **never uses AI** and would learn a new app only if her pay depended on it.
Her worries move from **unpaid mileage** in the calm pictures to **job loss** when robots arrive.
With little warning she'd **postpone the wedding** and save; with a decade she'd marry and start a family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots by 2031 leave her no time and no other training.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that families can always choose a **real carer**, and proper **mileage pay**.
Help moving into **care home work**, where she'd still be with people.
